title: SLO-centric multiplex router with capacity reservoirs and regional anchor leases
creator: Liam O'Neill
description: Design and implement a SLO-driven request multiplexing router that combines latency-based preference, geo-anchor leases (soft pinning), and a capacity-reservoir token system to make multi-region failover graceful and predictable. The router should expose controls for per-customer SLO weight, allow short-term capacity reservations (reservoirs) for bursty workloads, and integrate with circuit-breaker signals to trigger tiered shedding and fallback to compatible model variants.
acceptance_criteria: Router respects per-customer latency SLO weights and maintains <99th percentile tail within configured SLO budget under baseline traffic
Capacity reservoir mechanism prevents immediate cross-region stomping during short spikes and reduces cross-region egress by >= 25% in canary tests
Circuit-breaker integration results in prioritized shedding of non-critical routes and automatic fallback to cheaper model variant within 2s of breach detection
End-to-end telemetry and dashboards added: token-reservoir occupancy, geo-lease allocations, SLO burn-rate per region, and route-level failover counts
Rollout plan validated via canary (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%) with automated rollback criteria tied to tail latency and error-rate thresholds
notes: Motivation: current steering floods healthy regions during microbursts, causing noisy neighbor effects and higher egress costs. We need a short-horizon holdback (reservoir) that lets local region absorb bursts without immediate large-scale redistribution.
This ticket focuses on the routing layer only. Changes to autoscaling policies and scheduler are tracked separately (ENG-777778 will follow).
UX knobs: per-customer SLO weight (float), reservoir size (tokens), lease ttl and jitter, fallback model family mapping. Default sensible values will be provided by runtime profiles.
design_decisions: Use latency SLO weight (0..1) as primary scoring component, combined with capacity-reservoir score and geo-lease bonus to compute dispatch score
Reservoir implemented as token-bucket per-region-per-customer with short refill intervals (100ms granularity) to allow burst absorption while bounding sustained throughput
Geo-anchor leases are 'soft' leases: a short TTL (e.g., 30s) with randomized jitter so we avoid synchronized lease expirations across clients
Circuit-breaker state machine will emit events to router via existing event bus; router subscribes and reduces score for impacted endpoints and triages to fallback models and regional backups
Telemetry uses existing metrics pipeline; detailed histograms for token consumption and SLO-burn-rate will be exported with tags: region, model, customer_id, route
tradeoffs: Holding short reservoirs increases local latency under sustained load if autoscaler cannot react fast enough; mitigated by conservative reservoir sizing and fast autoscale hooks
Short lease TTLs reduce staleness but increase churn in routing decisions; we add jitter to reduce thundering herd
Computing richer scores per-request increases CPU in the dispatch plane; we plan to batch score computations and cache scores for short windows (50-200ms) to amortize cost
Fallback to cheaper model variants may change output quality; include quality guardrails and a model-variant confidence score to avoid unacceptable regressions
implementation_steps: 1) Extend router proto: add SLOWeight, ReservoirTokenBudget, LeaseMetadata fields
2) Implement reservoir token-bucket library (C++ runtime) with microbenchmarks and deterministic unit tests
3) Integrate reservoir accounting into scoring pipeline with short-lived in-memory caches
4) Wire circuit-breaker events to router subscription and define score degradation curve per-breaker-state
5) Add admin APIs to query and adjust reservoir sizes and lease parameters per-customer
6) Add telemetry instrumentation and Grafana dashboards (panel templates provided)
7) Create canary harness and synthetic scenarios that simulate regional microbursts and full-region outages
8) Iterate on default heuristics after canary data
telemetry_queries: Reservoir occupancy: sum(reservoir_tokens_used) by (region, customer) / sum(reservoir_capacity) by (region, customer)
SLO burn rate: increase(error_budget_consumed_percent) over 5m by (customer, region)
Tail latency per route: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route, region))
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Unit/integration tests and internal feature flag off (dev cluster)
Phase 1: Canary 1% on non-critical traffic profile for 48h; monitor reservoir occupancy and tail latency
Phase 2: Expand to 5% for 24h with synthetic microbursts introduced to validate behavior
Phase 3: 25% for 48h with automated rollback if 99th latency or error rate increases beyond thresholds
Phase 4: Full rollout with staged increases and post-rollout 7d observation
test_plan: Unit tests for reservoir token semantics (refill, borrow, steal prevention)
Integration tests where router receives circuit-breaker open events and shifts traffic to fallback models
Load tests: regional microburst scenario (10x for 10s) repeated over 1h to measure egress reduction and local tail latency
Chaos test: simulated regional outage to ensure graceful rebalancing and lease grief behavior
Quality regression: end-to-end evaluation comparing outputs when routing to primary vs fallback model (sampled by customer)
Canary asserts in CI to block rollout on regressions
risks: Incorrect reservoir sizing can cause increased latency or starvation for other tenants in the same region
Fallback model quality variance could produce unacceptable UX regressions for sensitive customers
Telemetry blind spots might delay detection of misrouting during rollout; require emergency dashboard guardrails
Routing score computation bugs could create oscillations between regions; mitigate with damping and min-stay windows
